haiku-low.q1: Only a SHA-256 hash is persisted, in api_tokens.token_hash. Plaintext appears only in the create response and the one-time dialog.
haiku-low.q2: They cannot. Once the dialog closes nobody can see the token again, so the user creates a new one.
haiku-low.q3: The server refuses with a 4xx telling the user to revoke a token first. Nothing is stored.
haiku-low.q4: On the very next API call that presents it, because the server reads the row each time and does not cache validity.
haiku-low.q5: The same generic 401 body in every case. The responses do not differ, so they do not reveal which failure occurred.
haiku-low.q6: The server hashes the bearer token with SHA-256 and looks up the row by hash. It is usable only if not revoked and not expired.
haiku-low.q7: A successful API call triggers it. It is written only if the stored value is empty or over 1 hour old, capping writes at one per hour.
haiku-low.q8: The API request still succeeds. The last-used time stays old until a later call writes it.
haiku-low.q9: Revoking sets the revoked time on that user's row. The list shows only active tokens, so the revoked token disappears from it.
haiku-low.q10: Another user's or nonexistent id returns 404 and changes nothing. Revoking an already-revoked token does nothing and still returns OK.
haiku-low.q11: The row exists, counts toward the 10-token limit, and the token can never be shown. The user revokes it from the list and creates a new one; it also expires after 90 days.

sonnet.q1: It stores only a SHA-256 hash (api_tokens.token_hash). The full plaintext appears only in the create response and the one-time dialog the user sees; never stored, logged or sent to analytics.
sonnet.q2: They can't. Nobody, including support and engineering, can see it again. The user must create a new token.
sonnet.q3: The server refuses with a 4xx and a message telling them to revoke a token first. Nothing is stored. (Open question: two simultaneous requests at 9 tokens could both succeed, making an 11th.)
sonnet.q4: On the very next API call, because the server reads the row every time and does not cache validity.
sonnet.q5: A 401 with the same generic body in every case (also for a missing header). The responses do not differ.
sonnet.q6: It hashes the presented token with SHA-256 and looks up the row by that hash. It then reads revoked and expires: the record is usable only if it is neither revoked nor expired.
sonnet.q7: A successful (valid) API call writes last-used only when the stored value is empty or more than 1 hour old. That rule limits writes to at most one per token per hour.
sonnet.q8: The API call still succeeds. The last-used time stays old until a later call writes it.
sonnet.q9: It sets a revoked time on the token's row (irreversible). The list selects only active tokens, so a revoked token no longer appears in the list.
sonnet.q10: Another user's token (or a nonexistent one) gets a 404 and nothing changes. An already-revoked token of the user's own does nothing and still returns OK, so retry is safe.
sonnet.q11: The row exists and counts toward the 10-token limit, but the token was never shown and can't be shown later. The user sees the name in the list, revokes it, and creates a new token. The row also expires on its own after 90 days.
